Text at the top reads: I opened the gate for the whole barn. Nobody said thank you. We're all in the feed room, so I'll assume it's gratitude.
posts.caption: The latch on the paddock gate has been wired shut twice and zip-tied once. Pudding treats it like a puzzle with a prize. Last Thursday I came out at 6:15 and found every stall door open and a line of horses outside the feed room, waiting like a church picnic. He stood at the front, calm, with oats on his nose. I counted heads, then bags. Nothing was missing but the lid off the oat bin and my confidence. I wired the gate a third time. The barn cat watched me do it and did not look hopeful.
posts.first: My husband bought a stronger latch on Saturday and called it horse-proof. Pudding studied it for about a minute on Sunday and went back to his hay. I think that's the most dangerous thing he's ever done. The old latch still hangs on the post as a reminder.

Text at the top reads: The farrier brought a new assistant to hold my foot. I let him hold it for two seconds. They both learned something.
posts.caption: The farrier has shod her for eleven years and still arrives at 7:40 with a coffee and a plan. This week he brought a young assistant, who stood very straight and was introduced to her left hind. Big Red lifted the foot politely, held it just long enough to be trusted, then set it down an inch from his boot. The farrier said that was about right and kept working. By eight she had her ears soft and her eyes half closed, like a woman at the salon. The assistant is coming back Thursday. He asked about steel-toed boots.
posts.first: I keep a spare hoof pick on a nail by her stall because the farrier always forgets his. He has borrowed it eleven times and returned it ten. Big Red noticed years ago and now stands a little taller whenever he reaches for it. I think she's keeping score.

posts.quote: Every barn has one bucket nobody remembers buying. It has outlasted three horses and two owners, and it has never once leaked.
posts.first: The blue one in our aisle came with the barn when we bought the place. The woman who sold it to us said it was basically new. That was 2014. I have filled it every morning since, and I have never asked where it came from.

posts.caption: His name is on the feed chart in my handwriting, and it has hung in the feed room longer than anyone else's. The paper curls at the corners and the blue ink has gone soft. Last spring a new boarder moved in with a nineteen-year-old mare and a lot of confidence. He gave her one slow look over the fence and went back to his hay. I never mentioned the birth years. She took the stall by the door. He kept the one by the window, and the sun finds it by noon.
posts.first: I wrote his name on that chart in blue marker the day he arrived, and I've traced over it every January since. Nobody else in the barn has the same blue. I have never replaced the pen. It lives in the drawer with the thermometer.

posts.caption: The photographer was booked for twenty minutes and I booked the Diva for the whole morning. I brushed, braided, oiled her hooves and found the one corner of the arena with good light. She held one pose for a full ten seconds, which is a record. Then a barn cat walked through the background and she turned to watch it, because nothing outranks a barn cat. The proofs came Tuesday. There is an ear, a fence rail and a very clean left hoof. I ordered the print anyway.
posts.first: I tried to hang the proof in the tack room and she knocked it off the nail twice. I think it was too honest. The ear picture lives in the kitchen now, next to the feed store calendar. My husband says it has character. He has never once said that about her forelock.

posts.caption: The barn lights are on a timer now, and the one in her stall is on its own switch. I did that last month after a night when the wind got loud and she would not lie down until two. The electrician came Friday, drank my coffee and called it a ten minute job. I didn't tell him it took me three weeks to decide. Now the light fades slowly after nine and she is asleep before it's gone. The cat sleeps on the hay bale under the switch.
posts.first: On windy nights I still walk out at ten and stand by her stall without saying anything. She doesn't wake up. The light is low and amber and the straw smells like July. I go back to the house and I sleep better than she does.
